title: Unashamed Witness to the Gospel of Life
summary: From prison Paul thanks God for Timothy’s sincere faith and urges him to rekindle God’s gift, suffer unashamed, and guard the entrusted gospel.
historicalContext: Second Timothy is Paul’s final letter, written from a Roman prison not long before his execution (4:6-8). This confinement was far harsher than the rented lodging of Acts 28. Paul wears a chain (1:16), a friend must search the city to find him (1:17), and at his first hearing no one stood beside him (4:16-17). The setting fits the years after the fire of Rome in A.D. 64, when Nero turned public suspicion against Christians and any open link with an imprisoned church leader carried real danger. Timothy was most likely still in Ephesus, the chief city of the province of Asia, where a wave of defection had shaken the believers (1:15) and corrupting teaching was still spreading (2:17-18). Paul writes to steady a younger colleague who is gifted yet inclined to timidity, and to hand on to him the gospel he must guard and teach once the apostle is gone.
literaryContext: The chapter joins a conventional letter opening to the themes of a farewell charge. A greeting (1:1-2) gives way to a thanksgiving filled with memory and centered on Timothy’s sincere faith (1:3-5). Paul then turns to direct appeal: rekindle the gift of God (1:6-7), refuse shame and share in suffering for the gospel (1:8), hold the pattern of sound words, and guard the good deposit (1:13-14). At the heart of the chapter stands a compact confession of the gospel (1:9-10), followed by Paul’s testimony of confidence in the God who keeps what is entrusted to Him “against that day” (1:11-12). The chapter closes with examples from Timothy’s own province: those in Asia who turned away, and Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of Paul’s chain (1:15-18). Repeated words such as shame, power, deposit, and that day bind the section together and prepare for the soldier, athlete, and farmer images of chapter 2.
themes: Power, love, and self-control from God’s Spirit
Unashamed partnership in suffering for the gospel
Grace purposed in eternity and revealed in Christ
Life and immortality as the gift of the gospel
Guarding the entrusted truth by the Holy Spirit

outline.title: An Apostle of the Promise of Life
outline.summary: Paul greets his beloved son Timothy as an apostle sent to announce the life God has promised in Christ Jesus.

outline.title: Thanksgiving for Unfeigned Faith
outline.summary: From prison Paul gives thanks, remembers Timothy’s tears, and rejoices in a sincere faith passed through Lois and Eunice.

outline.title: Rekindling the Gift of God
outline.summary: Timothy must fan into flame the gift he received, for God gives a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear.

outline.title: Unashamed of the Gospel That Conquers Death
outline.summary: Grounded in eternal grace revealed at Christ’s appearing, Paul calls Timothy to share his sufferings and testifies to God’s keeping power until that day.

outline.title: Holding and Guarding the Good Deposit
outline.summary: Timothy is to keep the pattern of sound words in faith and love and guard the entrusted gospel through the indwelling Holy Spirit.

outline.title: Deserters and a Faithful Friend
outline.summary: The defection of those in Asia contrasts with Onesiphorus, who sought Paul out in Rome and was not ashamed of his chain.

verses.bibleText: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul opens his final letter with the title he has carried since the Damascus road: “an apostle of Jesus Christ.” Timothy hardly needed the information. The title stands at the head because what follows is more than a farewell between friends. It is an apostolic charge that will govern Timothy’s ministry and, through him, the congregations in his care. The prisoner awaiting sentence in Rome still speaks with the authority of the risen Lord who sent him.

“By the will of God” places the origin of that authority outside Paul himself. He did not volunteer for apostleship or earn it by talent. God chose and commissioned him, and that settled conviction steadied him when nearly every human support had fallen away (1:15; 4:16). A calling that rests on the divine will cannot be cancelled by a cell or a verdict.

The next phrase names the purpose of his apostleship: “according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus.” Paul was sent to announce that God has pledged life and has located that life in His Son. The setting gives the words unusual force. Nero’s court could end Paul’s earthly existence, but it had no jurisdiction over the life God promised. That life begins now in union with Christ (Romans 6:4, 11) and reaches its fullness when the dead in Christ are raised incorruptible at His return (1 Corinthians 15:52-53). Paul does not speak of life as something humanity already holds by nature. It is promised, and it is “in Christ Jesus”; apart from Him there remains only the sentence of death that sin introduced.

The greeting therefore anticipates the gospel summary of verses 9-10, where Christ is said to have abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. A man facing the sword begins his last letter by speaking of life.

wordNotes.term: κατ’ ἐπαγγελίαν ζωῆς (kat’ epangelian zōēs) — according to the promise of life
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition expresses the aim toward which Paul’s apostleship is directed: he was commissioned in the service of what God has promised. In Paul’s letters God’s promise consistently centers on the salvation fulfilled in the Messiah. Here its content is life itself—fellowship with God now, and resurrection life that will never end.

wordNotes.term: ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en Christō Iēsou) — in Christ Jesus
wordNotes.explanation: This characteristic Pauline phrase recurs throughout the letter (1:9, 13; 2:1, 10; 3:12, 15). It identifies Christ as the sphere and source of the promised life. Life is not a general religious possession available apart from Him; it is found in union with His person.

verses.bibleText: To Timothy, my dearly beloved son: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Timothy is addressed as “my dearly beloved son.” In 1 Timothy and Titus Paul wrote of a “true” or “own” son in the faith, wording that stressed the legitimacy of the relationship. Here the accent falls on affection. Timothy had probably come to faith through Paul’s preaching at Lystra (Acts 14:6-7; 16:1-3), was trained at his side, and served with him “as a son with the father” (Philippians 2:22). Family language in the ancient world could describe formal obligations, yet Paul’s repeated longing to see Timothy (1:4; 4:9, 21) shows that the warmth here is unforced.

The blessing joins “grace, mercy, and peace.” Grace is God’s unearned favor, the fountain of every saving gift. Mercy is that same favor turned toward human weakness, guilt, and need. Peace is the wholeness and reconciliation that follow when grace has done its work. Mercy, added here as in 1 Timothy, suits a letter to a younger minister facing hardship, desertion, and opposition, for he would need compassion as much as strength.

These blessings come jointly “from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.” Paul places the Son beside the Father as the single source of divine blessing. The confession of Christ’s full deity is made almost in passing, as something already settled among believers. The Lord who will be named again and again in this letter is the One who shares the Father’s throne and dispenses His gifts.

wordNotes.term: ἀγαπητῷ τέκνῳ (agapētō teknō) — my dearly beloved son
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes a child, and in Paul’s usage it marks a spiritual relationship of conversion, training, and loyal partnership. The adjective “beloved” describes those whom God loves and whom believers therefore love in the Lord. Paul used the same pairing of Timothy when sending him to Corinth.

Mercy is God’s compassionate kindness toward the needy and undeserving. Paul’s own conversion was an experience of it, and in this chapter he will pray that Onesiphorus finds it in the day of judgment. Its place in the greeting reminds Timothy that ministry is sustained by divine compassion.

verses.bibleText: I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s thanksgiving rises from a prison where complaint would have seemed natural. He begins instead, “I thank God.” This is not a denial of hardship, for the letter will speak frankly of chains, desertion, and approaching death. Gratitude simply receives the first word, because the God Paul serves is still at work and Timothy is part of that work.

“Whom I serve from my forefathers” affirms continuity. Paul has not abandoned the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob for a new deity. Faith in Jesus as Messiah fulfills the hope his ancestors held (Acts 24:14; 26:6-7). The point carried weight in a Roman setting where the gospel could be dismissed as an illegal novelty, and it prepares for verse 5, where Timothy’s faith is also traced through his family. The verb Paul chooses is commonly used of worship; his entire ministry is offered to God as service.

“With pure conscience” is not a claim to sinlessness. Paul elsewhere calls himself the chief of sinners and recalls his violent opposition to the church (1 Timothy 1:13, 15). His conscience is clean because his sins have been forgiven and because he now serves without hidden motive or double life. Before the Sanhedrin he could say that he had lived before God in all good conscience (Acts 23:1). Under accusation, such a conscience becomes a source of courage rather than dread.

His remembrance of Timothy is constant: “without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day.” The phrase “night and day” describes the regular rhythm of a praying life, evening and morning, in which Timothy’s name keeps returning. Confined in Rome, Paul can no longer travel among the churches, but he can still intercede for them. Prayer was the one ministry no prison could shut down.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb is used in Scripture for the worship and religious service offered to God. Paul applies it to his whole apostolic life, presenting his preaching, suffering, and prayer as acts of worship. The present tense describes a settled, continuing pattern.

wordNotes.term: ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει (en kathara syneidēsei) — with pure conscience
wordNotes.explanation: Conscience is the inner awareness of one’s conduct as right or wrong before God. A “pure” or clear conscience belongs to one who has been cleansed by Christ and lives without concealed disloyalty. In the Pastorals it is closely tied to sincere faith and sound teaching.

verses.bibleText: Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The long sentence begun in verse 3 continues with a burst of longing: “greatly desiring to see thee.” The participle expresses strong yearning, the same Paul felt for believers in Rome, Philippi, and Thessalonica (Romans 1:11; Philippians 1:8; 1 Thessalonians 3:6). Later the desire will become an urgent request: “Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me” (4:9).

The memory of Timothy’s “tears” probably reaches back to their last parting, whether when Paul left him in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3) or at the time of Paul’s arrest. The detail is unguarded and personal. Timothy was no detached functionary but a man who felt the cost of separation keenly, and Paul does not treat those tears as weakness. The Ephesian elders had wept in the same way when Paul left them at Miletus (Acts 20:37-38).

Paul’s purpose is “that I may be filled with joy.” Tears and joy lie side by side in the sentence. Christian friendship does not erase the pain of parting, yet it carries the hope of reunion, and that hope changes the color of the sorrow. Even under sentence of death, Paul could still look forward to gladness.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes intense longing for someone or something absent. Paul uses it of his desire to see fellow believers and of the believer’s longing to be clothed with the resurrection body. Here it reveals the personal warmth behind his apostolic authority.

wordNotes.term: χαρᾶς πληρωθῶ (charas plērōthō) — I may be filled with joy
wordNotes.explanation: The passive form suggests a joy that comes as a gift rather than one manufactured by effort. Paul expects that reunion with Timothy, granted by God, will fill him completely, as he prayed that God would fill believers with all joy.

verses.bibleText: When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The thanksgiving reaches its focus in Timothy’s “unfeigned faith.” The adjective means literally “without hypocrisy,” a faith that is not worn like an actor’s mask. In a letter that will mention Demas, who loved this present world (4:10), and men who keep a form of godliness while denying its power (3:5), the sincerity of Timothy’s trust is no small matter. Paul’s whole appeal rests upon it: because Timothy’s faith is real, he can be summoned to stir up his gift and to suffer for the gospel.

The opening words may be read “when I call to remembrance” or, following a well-attested reading, “having been reminded.” The second suggests that recent news of Timothy had reached Paul, perhaps through a visitor. Either way, the memory moves him to thanks.

This faith “dwelt first” in Timothy’s grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Acts describes Eunice as a believing Jewish woman married to a Greek (Acts 16:1), and Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood in that home (3:15). Whether Lois and Eunice first trusted God as devout Jews who later welcomed Jesus as Messiah, or whether Lois believed the gospel first and the others followed, the line of influence is plain. The verb “dwelt” pictures faith taking up residence in a person, just as the Holy Spirit is said to dwell in believers in verse 14. Timothy’s father goes unmentioned, which hints at a household where spiritual instruction came mainly through the women.

Paul then adds, “and I am persuaded that in thee also.” Inherited faith is a gift, but it cannot replace personal faith. Lois and Eunice could teach and pray; they could not believe on Timothy’s behalf. The faith that lived in them now lives in him, and Paul is confident of it. Faithful instruction by parents and grandparents often bears fruit beyond what they live to see, and every child of a believing home must come to own that faith personally.

wordNotes.explanation: The adjective denies any element of play-acting. Unfeigned faith is trust in God that is the same in private as in public and does not shift with circumstances. Paul named it as one of the goals of his charge in 1 Timothy and uses the same quality to describe sincere love.

The verb means to live in or inhabit. Paul uses it of the indwelling Spirit, the indwelling word, and God dwelling among His people. Applied to faith, it presents trust in God as a settled presence that makes its home in a person’s life rather than a passing feeling.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore” ties the appeal to the sincere faith just described. Because Timothy’s faith is real, Paul can call on him to act upon it: “I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands.” The tone is that of a reminder rather than a rebuke. Paul assumes that Timothy knows what he must do and needs only to be roused to it.

The verb pictures a fire. It means to rekindle embers or to keep a flame burning at full strength. It does not require that Timothy’s fire had gone out; even a faithful worker facing opposition, loneliness, and the approaching loss of his mentor can let it burn low. The gift is neither replaced nor supplemented. It is already “in thee,” and Timothy is responsible for its use. God gives, and His servant must stir.

The “gift of God” is a charisma, a gracious endowment of the Spirit. Its connection with the laying on of hands links it to Timothy’s setting apart for ministry, which 1 Timothy 4:14 describes as accompanied by prophecy and the hands of the elders. Here Paul says “my hands,” for he shared in that commissioning and now writes as the one who stood beside Timothy at its beginning. The laying on of hands was the visible occasion; God was the giver. The act imparted no magical power, yet it marked a solemn recognition of God’s call and was accompanied by His equipping grace.

Every believer has received some gift for the service of the church (1 Peter 4:10). In hard seasons the temptation is to wait for a fresh endowment instead of faithfully using what God has already given. Paul’s counsel points the other way: return to the calling you received, and fan its flame.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to kindle afresh or keep a fire fully ablaze. The present tense suggests continuous tending rather than a single act. It places responsibility on Timothy to use and cultivate the gift God has already placed within him.

The word denotes a gift of grace, freely given by God. In Paul’s letters it often refers to an enabling of the Spirit for service in the body of Christ. Here it is the endowment fitted to Timothy’s ministry, received when he was set apart.

verses.bibleText: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear.” Paul explains why the gift must be stirred and why it can be. The word translated “fear” refers to timidity or cowardice, the shrinking that makes one draw back when faithfulness becomes costly; it occurs only here in the New Testament. Whatever Timothy’s natural temperament, timidity is not what God imparted to him. Fear of people, fear of disgrace, and fear of suffering do not come from the Spirit.

By writing “us,” Paul includes himself and all believers. The statement looks back to what God gave when He bestowed His Spirit, and the positive half of the sentence makes clear that the Holy Spirit is in view. He is the Spirit “of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” Each quality checks and completes the others.

Power is the Spirit’s strength, enabling weak servants to witness, endure, and stand firm (Acts 1:8; Ephesians 3:16). It is not domineering force. Paul pairs it at once with love, the first fruit of the Spirit, poured into believers’ hearts (Romans 5:5; Galatians 5:22). Power without love turns harsh; love without power becomes sentimental and ineffective. The third term, rendered “sound mind,” speaks of self-control, sober judgment, and disciplined thinking. It belongs to the word family Paul uses for the self-controlled overseer (1 Timothy 3:2) and for the sober estimate each believer must form of himself (Romans 12:3). It keeps zeal from sliding into fanaticism and courage from becoming recklessness, and it governs thought, appetite, and habit alike.

The verse does not promise that a believer will never feel afraid. Paul himself confessed to coming among the Corinthians “in fear, and in much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). Fear may arise, yet it is not the ruling spirit of the Christian life. The Spirit God gives enables His servants to do what is right in spite of their feelings.

Christ embodied this triad. He confronted His opponents with authority, wept over Jerusalem, and remained clear-minded before Pilate. The Spirit who rested on Him now dwells in His people, equipping them for courageous, loving, and balanced witness in a hostile world.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means cowardice or timidity, a fearfulness that leads to retreat from duty. It differs from reverent fear of God, which Scripture commends. Jesus rebuked a similar fearfulness in His disciples during the storm, and the book of Revelation lists the fearful among those who abandon faithfulness.

This word, used only here in the New Testament, combines the ideas of prudence, self-discipline, and sober judgment. Related words describe the self-controlled character required of church leaders and of believers generally. It is a gift of the Spirit, not merely the product of human effort.

verses.bibleText: Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Be not thou therefore ashamed.” The “therefore” draws the practical conclusion from verse 7: since God has given a spirit of power rather than timidity, Timothy must not be ashamed. The Greek construction typically forbids an action not yet begun. Paul is not accusing Timothy of cowardice; he is fortifying him against a temptation that would grow stronger as Paul’s situation worsened.

Two possible objects of shame are named. The first is “the testimony of our Lord,” the gospel message about Jesus. A crucified Messiah was foolishness to Greeks and an offense to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). In Rome, to proclaim as Lord a man executed under a Roman governor could appear both absurd and seditious. The second is “me his prisoner.” Imprisonment carried heavy social disgrace in the ancient world, and a friend of a condemned man might share his danger. Some in Asia had apparently distanced themselves from Paul for that very reason (1:15). Paul, however, calls himself the Lord’s prisoner. His chains are evidence of loyalty to Christ, and Christ remains sovereign over them (Ephesians 3:1; Philippians 1:12-14).

In place of shame Paul calls Timothy to fellowship in suffering: “be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel.” The compound verb, perhaps formed for the occasion, means to suffer hardship together with someone. Timothy is invited to stand beside Paul and to accept whatever the gospel costs. Suffering appears here as the normal companion of faithful witness in a world in rebellion against God (3:12), an expected part of discipleship rather than an unlucky accident.

This endurance is not achieved by willpower: “according to the power of God.” The same power of the Spirit named in verse 7 enables the sharing of hardship. Paul then pauses to describe the God whose power upholds His servants—the God who saved and called them (verse 9). The courage to stand with Christ grows from remembering what He has done.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes the embarrassment that makes a person distance himself from someone or something regarded as disgraceful. Jesus warned against being ashamed of Him and His words, and Paul declared that he was not ashamed of the gospel. The word links verses 8, 12, and 16 in this chapter.

wordNotes.term: συγκακοπάθησον (synkakopathēson) — be thou partaker of the afflictions
wordNotes.explanation: This compound joins “with” to “suffer evil,” meaning to endure hardship alongside another. It appears again in 2:3. The call is to solidarity: Timothy is to share willingly in the sufferings that come to those who proclaim Christ.

verses.bibleText: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The mention of God’s power unfolds into one of the fullest summaries of salvation in Paul’s letters. Verses 9 and 10 move from eternity to history and from God’s purpose to Christ’s triumph over death. They explain why Timothy can suffer without shame: the God who calls him to share hardship has already saved him.

God is the One “who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling.” Salvation is described as accomplished. Believers have been rescued from the guilt and dominion of sin and from the death it brings, though the full outworking awaits Christ’s heavenly kingdom (4:18). The call is God’s effective summons that brings a person to faith. It is “holy” because it comes from a holy God and because it leads to a holy life (1 Thessalonians 4:7; 1 Peter 1:15-16). God does not save people to leave them in their sins. Grace that pardons also transforms, and obedience to God’s commandments becomes the fruit of the new life rather than its price.

“Not according to our works.” Paul excludes human merit as the ground of salvation. No obedience, religious observance, or moral attainment earns God’s favor (Ephesians 2:8-9; Titus 3:5). Salvation rests instead on God’s “own purpose and grace.” His purpose is His saving plan; His grace is the undeserved love that moves Him to carry it out. Both are “his own,” originating in God and dependent on nothing outside Him.

This grace “was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,” literally “before times eternal.” Before human history unfolded and before sin appeared, God had already provided for redemption in His Son. The rebellion that began in heaven and spread to earth took Him by no surprise. The plan of salvation was the expression of a love that had resolved from eternity to meet sin at whatever cost, and no emergency measure devised after the Fall (Revelation 13:8; 1 Peter 1:19-20). The grace was given “in Christ”; He is the One in whom the plan was secured and through whom it is applied.

This eternal purpose is no arbitrary sorting of some for salvation and others for loss. God “will have all men to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), and through the gospel the call goes out to all. Those who answer it discover that their salvation rests on foundations older than the world.

wordNotes.term: κλήσει ἁγίᾳ (klēsei hagia) — an holy calling
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase may express the means of God’s saving action (“with a holy calling”) or its goal (“to a holy life”). Both ideas belong together: a holy God issues the call, and those who answer are summoned to walk worthy of it in purity and obedience.

wordNotes.term: πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων (pro chronōn aiōniōn) — before the world began
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “before times eternal,” the expression points back before the ages of earth’s history began. Paul uses similar language for the mystery of salvation kept in God’s counsel and the promise of eternal life given before time. It roots salvation in God’s settled purpose, not in human initiative.

verses.bibleText: But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The grace purposed in eternity “is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ.” The contrast between “before the world began” and “now” marks the turning point of history. What had been hidden in God’s counsel became visible in the incarnation, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. The word “appearing,” used elsewhere in the Pastorals for Christ’s glorious return (4:1, 8; Titus 2:13), here describes His first advent; the second appearing will complete what the first began.

Christ is the Savior “who hath abolished death.” The verb means to render powerless, to strip of effect. Christians still die, and Paul himself expected execution. Yet death has lost its final authority over those in Christ. Through His death and resurrection Jesus broke the power of the one who held the power of death (Hebrews 2:14-15). For the believer, death becomes a sleep from which Christ will awaken His people (John 11:11, 25; 1 Thessalonians 4:14). Its complete removal, the destruction of “the last enemy,” will take place at the resurrection when Christ returns (1 Corinthians 15:26, 54).

He has also “brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.” The word rendered “immortality” means incorruptibility, a life no longer subject to decay or death. Scripture does not present immortality as something humans possess by nature. God “only hath immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16). Since the Fall humanity has been mortal, subject to death because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12). Immortality is something believers are to “seek for” (Romans 2:7), and Paul specifies when it is conferred: at the last trumpet, when “this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53). Christ does not uncover an undying soul already present in everyone; He offers, through the gospel, a gift that was never human property.

“To light” pictures dawn breaking after a long night. The hope of resurrection was present in the Old Testament (Job 19:25-27; Daniel 12:2), yet it was seen only dimly. At Christ’s empty tomb that hope stands in full daylight. Through the proclaimed gospel that light reaches every hearer who believes.

For Paul in his cell this truth carried immediate weight. The empire could take his breath, but it could not touch the life Christ had secured for him. He could face the executioner calmly because death had already been defeated and the morning of resurrection was certain. That same hope belongs to every believer who falls asleep in Jesus.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to make ineffective, nullify, or bring to nothing. Paul uses it for the destruction of death as the last enemy and for Christ’s defeat of the devil’s power. The aorist views Christ’s victory as accomplished at the cross and empty tomb, though its final display awaits the resurrection at His coming.

The noun means incorruptibility, the condition of being no longer subject to decay and death. In Paul it describes the resurrection state of the redeemed, put on when the dead are raised, and something believers seek rather than already possess. It is a gift brought to light through the gospel, not an innate property of human nature.

verses.bibleText: Whereunto I am appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Whereunto I am appointed” looks back to the gospel just described. Paul did not appoint himself; the passive verb implies that God placed him in this service, as he says in nearly the same words in 1 Timothy 2:7. Timothy had no doubts about Paul’s commission. Reflection on the greatness of the gospel simply leads Paul to marvel again that he, once a persecutor, should have been entrusted with it.

Three titles describe one ministry. As “a preacher,” Paul is a herald, publicly announcing what God has done in Christ. As “an apostle,” he is a commissioned envoy who saw the risen Lord and was sent with His authority. As “a teacher,” he instructs converts in the meaning and claims of the gospel so that faith matures into understanding and obedience. Timothy shares two of these roles: he must preach the word (4:2) and teach faithful men (2:2), though he is not an apostle.

The words “of the Gentiles” are missing here from several important early manuscripts and were probably added from 1 Timothy 2:7. The truth they express stands either way: Paul was the Lord’s chosen vessel to carry His name to the nations (Acts 9:15).

wordNotes.explanation: A herald was an official messenger who publicly proclaimed the decree or announcement of a ruler. Applied to Paul, it stresses that his message was not his own opinion but the King’s proclamation. Noah is given the same title in 2 Peter.

The teacher explains, applies, and grounds believers in the truth. Paul uses the title of himself only here and in 1 Timothy 2:7, perhaps to model for Timothy the teaching responsibility that will be central to his own work.

verses.bibleText: For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For the which cause I also suffer these things.” Paul’s sufferings are the direct consequence of his appointment as herald of the gospel. “These things” gathers up his imprisonment, his chain, the charge of criminal conduct, and the prospect of death. He accepts them as belonging to his calling.

“Nevertheless I am not ashamed.” Here Paul models what he asked of Timothy in verse 8. Treated as an evildoer before an empire, he neither hides his identity nor softens his message. Christ Himself endured the cross, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), and the three Hebrews before Nebuchadnezzar stood firm whether or not God chose to deliver them (Daniel 3:16-18). Paul stands in that company.

The ground of his confidence is personal: “for I know whom I have believed.” He does not say “what,” though he cares intensely about sound doctrine. His certainty rests on a Person he has known and trusted for some three decades. The perfect tense of “believed” describes trust begun in the past and still continuing. Paul’s knowledge of God has been tested by shipwreck, stoning, and prison, and found sure.

He is “persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.” The Greek reads literally “my deposit,” and the phrase can be understood two ways. It may refer to what Paul has entrusted to God: his life, his whole person, his future, and his labor. Or it may refer to what God entrusted to Paul, the gospel itself, as the same word means in verse 14 and 1 Timothy 6:20. The emphasis on God as guardian, together with the personal “my,” favors the first reading here, while the second follows in verse 14 as Timothy’s charge. Both convictions upheld Paul: God would keep him, and God would keep the gospel.

“Against that day” points to the day of Christ’s appearing and judgment (1:18; 4:8). Paul does not expect to enter his reward at the moment of execution. He commits himself to God as a depositor places treasure with a reliable keeper, confident that it will be returned intact on the appointed day. Death may lay him in the grave, yet nothing he has committed to God is lost. At the resurrection the Lord will raise His servant and give him the crown laid up for him (4:8). Every believer may make the same commitment and rest in the same assurance.

wordNotes.term: παραθήκην (parathēkēn) — that which I have committed
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes property placed in another’s care for safekeeping, a deposit that must be returned intact. In the Pastorals it appears only with the verb “guard.” Here, with God as guardian and the possessive “my,” it most naturally describes what Paul has entrusted to God, though it is closely tied to the gospel deposit Timothy must guard.

wordNotes.term: ἐκείνην τὴν ἡμέραν (ekeinēn tēn hēmeran) — that day
wordNotes.explanation: In this letter “that day” is the day of Christ’s appearing, when He judges and rewards His people. The expression echoes the Old Testament day of the Lord and Jesus’ own use of it for the final reckoning. It fixes the believer’s reward at Christ’s return rather than at death.

verses.bibleText: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul turns from his own testimony to direct charge: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me.” The word translated “form” means a pattern, outline, or standard, like an architect’s sketch or a model to be copied. What Timothy heard from Paul is to serve as the governing standard for all his teaching. He is not to replace it with novelties or treat it as a loose suggestion. He may illustrate, apply, and expand it, yet always within its lines.

The “sound words” are healthy words, teaching that produces spiritual health in contrast to the diseased speculation that spreads like gangrene (2:17). The medical image runs throughout the Pastorals: true doctrine nourishes godliness, while error corrupts. Paul’s gospel was no invention of his own; he received it by revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:11-12), and so its pattern carries divine authority.

The pattern was heard “of me.” Timothy had listened to Paul in synagogues, homes, and assemblies over many years, “among many witnesses” (2:2). That body of apostolic teaching, now preserved in Scripture, remains the standard by which the church tests every message.

Paul then names the manner in which the pattern must be held: “in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.” Orthodoxy can be defended coldly or combatively, and when it is, the truth itself is misrepresented. Faith keeps the teacher dependent on God; love keeps him gentle toward those he instructs and even toward opponents (2:24-25). Both virtues are found “in Christ Jesus,” flowing from union with Him rather than from natural temperament. Sound words held in a sour spirit contradict the gospel they claim to defend.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means an outline, model, or pattern that sets the standard for what follows. Paul used it of his own conversion as a pattern for later believers. Here the apostolic teaching is the template to which Timothy’s preaching must conform, allowing application without alteration of substance.

The participle comes from a verb meaning to be in good health. Sound words are wholesome teaching that promotes spiritual health and godly living. The Pastorals repeatedly set such teaching against unhealthy disputes that breed strife and corrupt faith.

verses.bibleText: That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“That good thing which was committed unto thee keep.” The verse restates and deepens the charge of verse 13. The “good thing” is the deposit, the same word used in verse 12. There God guards what Paul committed to Him; here Timothy must guard what God has committed to him. The deposit is the gospel in its apostolic form, the pattern of sound words just mentioned, together with the ministry of proclaiming it. It is called “good” because it is precious, true, and beneficial.

The verb “keep” means to guard, as a sentry protects what is under his watch. Teachers in Ephesus were already distorting the faith, denying the future resurrection (2:18) and turning hearers toward fables (4:4). Paul’s own guardianship of the truth was nearly finished. Custody now passed to Timothy and, through him, to faithful men who would teach others also (2:2).

No minister can do this in his own strength. The guarding is to be done “by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.” The Spirit who inspired the truth also preserves it, illuminating the mind, strengthening conviction, and giving discernment to recognize error. The phrase “in us” includes Paul and Timothy and, more broadly, all believers, for the Spirit dwells in every child of God (Romans 8:9-11). Fidelity to the truth is therefore a work of grace as well as a duty.

Christians today hold the same trust. The faith once delivered to the saints (Jude 1:3) has been placed in the church’s keeping, and each generation must guard it, live it, and hand it on unchanged.

wordNotes.term: τὴν καλὴν παραθήκην φύλαξον (tēn kalēn parathēkēn phylaxon) — that good thing which was committed unto thee keep
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative “guard” calls for vigilant protection against loss or damage. The deposit is the gospel entrusted to Timothy, described as “good” for its worth and truth. The same charge closes 1 Timothy, showing how central the faithful custody of apostolic teaching was to Paul’s final instructions.

The participle describes the Spirit as a resident presence within believers. Paul uses the same verb of the Spirit who will quicken mortal bodies at the resurrection and of the word of Christ dwelling richly in the church. The indwelling Spirit is the power behind faithful guardianship.

verses.bibleText: This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now turns to examples drawn from Timothy’s own region. “This thou knowest” assumes the event was common knowledge in Ephesus. “All they which are in Asia be turned away from me.” Asia is the Roman province of western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its leading city—the region where Paul had labored for nearly three years and from which the word had spread so widely (Acts 19:10).

The “all” cannot mean every believer in the province, since Timothy himself and the household of Onesiphorus remained loyal. It most likely refers to a particular group, perhaps leaders or co-workers, who failed Paul at a moment of crisis—possibly at his arrest, or when they were asked to stand by him in Rome. The verb describes a turning away from Paul personally. Whether it also meant abandoning the faith is not stated, though disowning the Lord’s prisoner sits uncomfortably close to being ashamed of the Lord’s testimony (1:8).

Two men are named, Phygellus and Hermogenes, and nothing more is known of them. Their names survive only as a warning, a sobering instance of how a person may be remembered for a single act of desertion. Their failure supplies the dark background against which Onesiphorus shines, and it sharpens Paul’s appeal that Timothy not follow their path. Loyalty to Christ often shows itself in loyalty to His suffering servants.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to turn away from or reject. In Titus it describes people who turn from the truth, and later in this letter hearers who turn their ears from it. Here the immediate object is Paul himself, a personal desertion that nonetheless endangered the cause he represented.

wordNotes.term: ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ (en tē Asia) — in Asia
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase refers to the Roman province occupying the western part of modern Turkey, whose principal city was Ephesus. Paul’s long ministry there had made Asia a center of the gospel, which made this defection especially painful.

verses.bibleText: The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Against the bleak backdrop of desertion Paul sets one bright example: “The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus.” The name means “profit-bringer,” and he lived up to it. Paul prays first for his household, perhaps because Onesiphorus was away from home when he served Paul in Rome while his family remained in Ephesus (4:19). The prayer echoes Jesus’ beatitude, “Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). Those who showed mercy to Paul are commended to the mercy of the Lord.

“For he oft refreshed me.” The verb suggests reviving someone with fresh air or cool relief. Whether Onesiphorus brought food, clothing, or simply his company, his visits were like clean air in a foul prison. Repeated visits imply sustained commitment rather than a single gesture.

Most striking of all, he “was not ashamed of my chain.” The word for “ashamed” links Onesiphorus directly with Paul’s charge to Timothy in verse 8 and with Paul’s own testimony in verse 12. Here is the model in flesh and blood: a believer who openly associated himself with a chained prisoner when doing so was dangerous. The “chain” is probably literal; Paul was physically bound. To visit him was to be seen with a man the authorities regarded as a criminal.

Christ counts such ministry as done to Himself: “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Matthew 25:36). Visiting those who suffer for righteousness remains one of the clearest evidences that faith has become love in action.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to cool, revive, or give breathing room. A related noun describes the “times of refreshing” from the Lord. Onesiphorus brought relief and renewed vigor to a weary prisoner through his presence and practical help.

The word denotes a literal chain or fetter, used for binding prisoners. Paul referred to his chain before the Jewish leaders in Rome and called himself an ambassador in bonds. Not being ashamed of it meant accepting public association with his disgrace.

verses.bibleText: But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me.” Onesiphorus did not wait for Paul to find him. Arriving in the capital, perhaps on business, he made it his aim to locate the apostle. In a vast city, with prisoners held in various places and Christians under suspicion after the fire, the search demanded persistence and courage. Inquiring after a condemned Christian leader could expose the inquirer to the same suspicion.

The verbs mark the stages: he sought, and he found. The adverb “very diligently” describes earnest, determined effort. This is the only place in the letter where Rome is named as the site of Paul’s imprisonment.

The contrast with Paul’s earlier Roman imprisonment is evident. Then he lived in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to him (Acts 28:30-31). Now he had to be searched out. Onesiphorus’s diligence reflects the persistent love of the Shepherd who goes after the lost sheep until He finds it (Luke 15:4).

wordNotes.explanation: The adverb describes eager, earnest effort. Paul uses the same word when urging Titus to help travelers on their way with care. It conveys an energetic devotion that refuses to give up until the task is done.

wordNotes.term: ἐζήτησεν… καὶ εὗρεν (ezētēsen… kai heuren) — sought… and found
wordNotes.explanation: The paired verbs describe a search carried through to success. The simple sequence recalls the language of Jesus about seeking and finding, and it prepares for Paul’s wordplay in the next verse, where the one who found Paul is to find mercy.

verses.bibleText: The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul interrupts his account with a second prayer: “The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day.” There is a play on words. The man who “found” Paul in Rome (verse 17) is to “find” mercy at the judgment. The double mention of “Lord” may refer first to Christ and then to the Father, or it may repeat the divine name for emphasis. Either way, the mercy comes wholly from God.

“That day” is, as in verse 12 and 4:8, the day of Christ’s appearing, when He judges the living and the dead (4:1). Paul does not suggest that Onesiphorus earns salvation by kindness. He prays that he will find mercy, which by definition is undeserved. At the same time, Jesus taught that the judgment will disclose whether faith expressed itself in love toward His needy brethren (Matthew 25:34-40). Onesiphorus’s care for Paul was the fruit of living faith, and Paul longs to see it acknowledged on that day.

Because Onesiphorus’s household is mentioned separately both here and in 4:19, some have concluded that he had died and that this verse is a prayer for the dead. The text does not require that conclusion; he may simply have been away from his family when Paul wrote. Even if he had died, Paul’s words voice a hope directed toward the day of judgment rather than a petition to change a departed person’s state. Scripture presents the dead as resting in the sleep of death until the resurrection (John 5:28-29; 1 Thessalonians 4:16) and gives no warrant for prayers on their behalf. The wish looks forward to Christ’s return, when the faithful are raised and rewarded together.

Paul closes by recalling “in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.” The words “unto me” are missing from some manuscripts, so the service may have reached the church more broadly. Timothy had seen it firsthand. Onesiphorus’s kindness in Rome was the continuation of a life of service at home.

wordNotes.explanation: To find mercy is to receive God’s undeserved compassion, here at the final judgment. Hebrews invites believers to come boldly to obtain mercy, and Jude urges them to look for the mercy of Christ unto eternal life. The phrase keeps grace at the center even where faithful service is in view.

The verb means to serve or render practical help, and it belongs to the same family as the word for deacon. It covers many kinds of service, from material support to personal care, and Jesus applied it to His own life of giving.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What makes a person reluctant to be openly associated with Christ or with those who suffer for Him?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Because God has saved us by grace, broken the power of death, and promised immortal life in Christ, His servants can suffer unashamed and guard the gospel by the Spirit’s power.
discussionQuestions: How does Paul distinguish inherited faith from personal faith in verse 5?
What does it mean to “stir up” a gift God has already given?
Why does Paul attach a summary of salvation (1:9-10) to his call to share in suffering (1:8)?
How does 1:10 shape our understanding of death, immortality, and the resurrection?
What does Onesiphorus teach about loyalty when association with the faithful is costly?
commonMisunderstandings: Rekindling the gift does not imply that Timothy had lost his faith; Paul urges him to keep a God-given gift burning at full strength.
“Life and immortality” brought to light does not mean that every person already has an immortal soul; immortality is God’s gift through the gospel, conferred on the redeemed at the resurrection.
Paul’s wish that Onesiphorus find mercy “in that day” does not establish prayer for the dead; it looks ahead to the judgment and reward at Christ’s appearing.
Holding fast sound words does not license harsh orthodoxy; Paul requires that the truth be held in faith and love.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God’s action and the believer’s responsibility together: God gives the Spirit, grace, and keeping power, and Timothy must rekindle, suffer, hold fast, and guard.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Entrust your life to the God who has conquered death, and stand unashamed with Christ and His people, guarding His truth by the Spirit until that day.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s eternal grace, revealed in the appearing of Christ, breaks the power of death and offers life and immortality as a gift through the gospel.
flow: Sin brought death, and no human effort can reverse it.
Before time began God purposed to save by grace rather than by our works.
Christ appeared, stripped death of its power, and brought life and immortality to light.
Immortality is given to those in Christ when He returns and the dead are raised.
Those who receive this gift can face suffering and even death unashamed.
simpleIllustrations: A trustworthy guardian keeps a deposit safe until the owner returns to claim it; God keeps the life entrusted to Him until the resurrection morning.
Embers that look dim can be fanned back into flame; God’s gift needs stirring, not replacing.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you entrust your life to the One who has abolished death and offers immortality through the gospel?
cautions: Do not present immortality as a natural possession of every human being; Scripture presents it as God’s gift in Christ.
Do not imply that suffering for the gospel earns salvation; faithful endurance flows from grace already received.
Do not shame timid believers; Paul strengthens Timothy with encouragement and reminders of God’s power.

reflectionQuestions: Is my faith my own, or am I still leaning on the faith of those who taught me?
What gift has God given me that I have allowed to burn low?
Where am I tempted to be ashamed of Christ or of His suffering people?
Have I entrusted my life and future to the God who will keep it until that day?
Who near me needs the kind of costly, seeking loyalty Onesiphorus showed Paul?
